title: Steamed Egg Custard
subtitle: Silky savoury steamed egg with soy sauce and sesame oil
excerpt: Beaten eggs are mixed with warm stock in a specific ratio and steamed over a very low heat until they set into a trembling, silky custard with no bubbles or holes. It is finished with a drizzle of light soy sauce and sesame oil. The technique is simple but the temperature control is critical. Serves 4 in about 25 minutes.
sourceNotes: Steamed egg custard, known in Chinese as zheng shui dan, is one of the most common home-cooked dishes across China, eaten as part of a rice meal or on its own as a light dish. It appears in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Every Grain of Rice' (Bloomsbury, 2012), where she describes it as a comfort food found in households across the country, and in Yan-Kit So's 'Classic Food of China' (Macmillan, 1992), which discusses the critical importance of the egg-to-liquid ratio and steaming temperature for achieving the smooth, hole-free texture.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Chinese savoury egg dish made by whisking eggs with warm stock and steaming the mixture until it sets into a smooth, trembling custard. Unlike baked or boiled egg dishes, steaming at a controlled temperature produces a silky, hole-free texture. The dish is eaten with rice and seasoned only at the table with soy sauce and sesame oil.

The proportion of stock to egg is the most critical variable in steamed egg custard. Too little stock and the custard is rubbery; too much and it will not set. The standard ratio is 1 part beaten egg to 1.5 to 2 parts warm stock by volume. Measuring by volume rather than weight is more reliable.

A thin, pale soy sauce with a clean, salty flavour used as a seasoning and table condiment. For steamed egg custard it is drizzled over the finished dish rather than cooked into it, so its fresh, delicate flavour comes through clearly. Dark soy sauce is not suitable here.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 as a side dish and takes about 25 minutes. The
sets in 12 to 14 minutes over a gentle steam. Too much heat causes bubbles and a pitted, spongy surface. Low and slow is essential.

is the make-or-break variable. Measure the beaten egg by volume in a jug, then add 1.5 times that volume of warm (not hot) stock. Sieve the mixture into the dish to remove air bubbles and any stringy egg white. Cover the dish with cling film or a plate before steaming to stop condensation dripping onto the surface.
Beat the {{eggs}} gently with a fork or chopsticks, trying not to incorporate too much air. Measure the beaten egg in a jug. Note the volume.
Add 1.5 times that volume of warm {{warm-chicken-stock}} to the egg. Add the {{light-soy-sauce}}, salt and white pepper. Stir gently to combine.
Pass the mixture through a fine sieve into a shallow heatproof dish. Skim any surface foam with a spoon. Cover the dish tightly with cling film or a flat plate.

Set the dish in a steamer over barely simmering water. The water should not be at a rolling boil. Steam over a very low heat for 12 to 14 minutes. The custard is ready when the edges are set and the centre wobbles only slightly when the dish is moved.

Remove the cover carefully to avoid letting condensation drip onto the surface. Drizzle with {{light-soy-sauce}} and {{sesame-oil}} and scatter with sliced spring onions. Serve straight from the dish.

items.symptom: The surface is pitted with holes and the texture is spongy
items.cause: The steam was too vigorous or the egg mixture had too many air bubbles
items.fix: Steam over a bare simmer with the lid slightly ajar if your steamer runs very hot. Sieve the mixture and rest it for 5 minutes before cooking to let air bubbles surface and pop.

items.symptom: The custard is watery and has not set
items.cause: Too much stock relative to egg, or not enough steaming time
items.fix: Check the ratio: 1 part beaten egg to 1.5 parts stock by volume. Cover the dish again and steam for another 3 to 4 minutes.

items.symptom: The custard is rubbery and dense
items.cause: The stock was too hot when added, partially cooking the egg, or the ratio had too little stock
items.fix: The stock should be warm but comfortable to touch, around 50°C. Use a full 1.5 to 2 parts stock per part egg.

content.text: Steamed egg custard is a quiet, everyday dish eaten across China as part of a shared rice meal. It is especially common as a dish for the elderly, for children, or for anyone who needs something easy to digest. The

and sesame oil added at the table are the only seasoning it needs. Regional variations include adding minced pork, prawns or preserved vegetables to the dish before steaming, but the plain version remains the most widely eaten.
